newsitem.title: BELGIUM: SOCCER-ANDERLECHT OUT TO RESTORE PRIDE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ANDERLECHT OUT TO RESTORE PRIDE.

text.p: Belgian soccer powerhouse Anderlecht are determined to silence the critics and repair a dented image by landing their 25th league title in the new season kicking off on Friday.
"It's true, 1996-97 has been a very bad season," club president Roger Vanden Stock said.
The season was marked by humiliating defeats and mediocre performances and they only salvaged a UEFA Cup place in the dying minutes of the season.
"If Anderlecht win the title, it's considered normal. When they finish runners-up, the atmosphere here is like at a club that is being relegated," club manager Michel Verschueren said.
To make matters worse, the club's image was tarnished by match-fixing allegations and their leading striker Gilles De Bilde suspended for punching an opponent in the face.
But Vanden Stock said Anderlecht had worked hard to turn the tide and felt armed for a shot at the title.
"The expectations are high, we have made a very big effort to strengthen ourselves," he said.
Anderlecht have made eight signings, including Belgium captain and former Anderlecht player Enzo Scifo, who was transferred from Monaco together with Dane Dan Petersen.
"Scifo's return has sparked some kind of metamorphosis at this club," said Verschueren, adding Scifo's comeback after a decade abroad had helped facilitate the other transfers.
"All the other transfer negotiations did not take more than half an hour," Verschueren said.
On Monday, Anderlecht also completed their long search for a new striker when they signed Liberian international James Debbah from French second division team Nice.
Anderlecht named former Belgium international defender Rene Vandereycken as successor for their Dutch coach Johan Boskamp whose impact on the Anderlecht team had been rapidly waning last season.
But despite all the changes and renewed ambition, rival first division clubs still remain to be convinced that Anderlecht are the main title pretenders.
A survey of first division coaches by the Humo magazine on Tuesday showed 11 coaches believed Club Bruges would lift the title. Anderlecht won four votes, Standard Liege one.
Nobody voted for outgoing champions Lierse, who saw the bulk of the team leave in lucrative transfers and appear to have squandered their title chances even before the start of the season.
Even Anderlecht were repeatedly confronted by their budget restrictions and continually drew the shortest straw in recent months in transfer negotiations for a new striker.
"More and more our problem is that our budget of 750 million francs ($19.3 million) is not enough to compete with the big ones like Juventus, Real Madrid, Milan or Barcelona," Verschueren said.
"There are clubs with a budget of three, four, five, even six billion francs ($77.3 to 154.6 million)," he said.
Most Belgian first division clubs have a budget of less than 150 million francs ($3.9 million).

To keep up with Europe's main clubs, Anderlecht are almost forced to qualify for the lucrative European Cup Champions' League which would inject the necessary funds to buy new players, or enable it to hold on to the ones it has by matching foreign offers.
"Even for Anderlecht it is not normal that there are just three players left in the team from our squad of 25 from three years ago," Vanden Stock said.
"We are traditionalists, we really like to keep our players."
